title: Middle East Oil Exports Rebound to Near Pre-War Levels as Crude Prices Stay Volatile
excerpt: Crude flows from the Gulf have recovered to about 98% of pre-war levels through overland pipelines and ship-to-ship transfers, but Brent prices remain volatile near $97–102 as tanker attacks continue and the U.S. sends a third carrier group to the region.
body:
• Middle East crude exports have rebounded to roughly 98% of pre-war levels, with J.P. Morgan estimating 17.5 million barrels a day on a 10-day average and Kpler reporting 16.5 million bpd leaving the region in September.
  • The recovery rests on workarounds, not peace: about 40% of Gulf crude now bypasses the Strait of Hormuz via Saudi and Emirati overland pipelines, and most tankers cross the strait with transponders off, transferring cargo ship-to-ship off Oman and Fujairah.
  • Oil prices remain volatile despite the restored flows: Brent fell below $100 to around $97 a barrel on October 1, but climbed back above $102 the same day on reports the U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier to the region.
  • Markets doubt the recovery can last without a lasting settlement: at least three tankers were attacked in the strait this week, and President Trump is reportedly considering resuming strikes on Iran after the November midterms.

Seven months after U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran upended Gulf energy flows, Middle East crude exports have staged a remarkable comeback — almost entirely on adapted logistics rather than diplomacy. At least 17.5 million barrels a day are now moving out of the region on a 10-day average, roughly 98% of pre-war levels, according to J.P. Morgan analysts cited by Dow Jones, while trade intelligence firm Kpler put September flows at 16.5 million bpd, matching pre-war averages excluding Iran.

That is a dramatic recovery from the low of 10.5 million bpd recorded in March, in the opening weeks of the conflict that began on February 28. But analysts caution the restored volumes mask a fragile arrangement: crude is getting out because exporters found ways around the disruption, not because the disruption has ended.

About 40% of the region's crude is now transported without transiting the Strait of Hormuz at all, compared with just 17% before the war, using Saudi and Emirati overland pipelines. Saudi Arabia restarted its east-west pipeline in late September after repairs from drone attacks, allowing exports to resume from the Red Sea port of Yanbu. What still crosses the strait increasingly does so in the dark: most shipments travel on tankers with their satellite transponders switched off, with over 70% of crude passing through the waterway in August changing tankers — up from almost none before the conflict — via ship-to-ship transfers off Oman and Fujairah.

Context & Background

Since the conflict began, Tehran has sought to exert authority over the Strait of Hormuz and at times declared it closed, choking the waterway that historically carried a huge share of the world's seaborne crude. Iran's control has declined as exporters built workarounds — naval escorts, pipelines, and the "dark fleet" of very large crude carriers running with transponders off.

The price story has been one of war-risk premium, not actual shortages. Brent crude rose about 14% in September — its biggest monthly gain since July — as traders priced in disruption fears, while WTI gained about 5%. A Wall Street Journal survey of bank forecasts, including Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan and Morgan Stanley, now puts Brent at an average of $90.22 a barrel in the fourth quarter, up sharply from previous estimates near $79.

Thursday's trading showed both forces at work. Prices fell in early trading — Brent down 0.7% to $97.30 and WTI down 0.9% to $89.60 — as investors weighed revived U.S.-Iran talks, brokered through Qatari shuttle diplomacy, against signs of recovering exports. Later in the day, prices surged after the Journal reported the Pentagon is deploying a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, plus as many as 10,000 sailors and Marines to the region, with forces expected by the end of November. December Brent gained 4.4% to $102.31.

Impact & Analysis

The comeback proves the Gulf's export machine can route around blockades — but it has not convinced markets the risk is over. As one MUFG analyst put it, regional crude flows have returned to pre-war levels, yet refined-product supply remains significantly tighter, and U.S. distillate stocks sit 14% below their five-year average. Speculation that President Trump expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterm elections has traders believing no lasting resolution comes until after the new year.

Macquarie energy strategist Walt Chancellor summed up the consensus caution: "We struggle to see a timely, comprehensive, and lasting resolution to the conflict emerging." That view is visible in the violence: at least three tankers were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz this week, while Iran and its Houthi allies have also targeted regional refineries. The recovery is real, but it is built on ship-to-ship transfers, dark tankers and overland pipelines — all arrangements that function only until the shooting escalates again.

"We struggle to see a timely, comprehensive, and lasting resolution to the conflict emerging."

— Walt Chancellor, Energy Strategist, Macquarie Group

Diaspora Angle

The Gulf's crude matters directly to India, which imports the bulk of its oil from the region: a sustained export recovery would ease India's import bill and take pressure off fuel prices and the rupee, while any renewed disruption hits Indian households and the government's finances first.

What's Next

Markets are watching three things: whether the Qatar-mediated U.S.-Iran talks produce anything concrete — President Trump has denied reports he would offer sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds; whether the arriving U.S. carrier group escalates or deters; and whether tanker attacks continue. If the export workarounds hold through the fourth quarter, Brent's forecast average of around $90 suggests the worst of the price spike may be over — provided the war stays contained.
